'''Robert Anthony Holton''' (January 26, 1944 – May 21, 2025) was an American chemist and academic renowned for his pioneering work in the chemical synthesis of the anti-cancer drug [[Taxol]] (paclitaxel). Holton’s research enabled large-scale production of Taxol, transforming cancer treatment and saving countless lives.<ref name="FSUnews">{{cite web |last=Haughney |first=Kathleen |title=FSU mourns loss of esteemed chemist who synthesized life-saving cancer drug Taxol |url=https://news.fsu.edu/news/science-technology/2025/06/03/fsu-mourns-loss-of-esteemed-chemist-who-synthesized-life-saving-cancer-drug-taxol/ |publisher=Florida State University News |date=June 3, 2025 |accessdate=June 3, 2025}}</ref> He was a professor of chemistry at [[Florida State University]] (FSU) and is widely recognized for achieving the first total synthesis of Taxol, a landmark accomplishment in synthetic organic chemistry.<ref name="FSUnews" />

== Early life and education ==
The son of Aaron T. and Marion ({{nee}} Downing) Holton, Robert Holton was born in [[Fayetteville, North Carolina]] on January 26, 1944, and raised in Charlotte.<ref name="nytimes" /><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bevisfh.com/obituaries/robert-holton-5/#!/Obituary |title=Obituary for Dr. Robert Anthony Holton |publisher=Bevis Funeral Home & Crematory}}</ref><ref name="LegacyObit">{{cite web |title=Dr. Robert Anthony Holton Obituary (1944–2025) |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/name/robert-holton-obituary?id=58519472 |publisher=Legacy.com |date=May 2025 |accessdate=June 3, 2025}}</ref> He was the son of Marion Downing Holton and Aaron T. Holton.<ref name="LegacyObit" /> He earned his undergraduate degree in chemistry from the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]], where he met his first wife, Juanita Bird.<ref name="LegacyObit" /> After moving to Tallahassee, he earned his doctorate from Florida State University and welcomed his first son, Robert.<ref name="LegacyObit" />

Following postdoctoral work at [[Stanford University]], during which time his second son, David, was born, Holton held faculty positions at [[Purdue University]] and [[Virginia Tech]].<ref name="LegacyObit" /> In 1986, he returned to FSU with his second wife, Marie E. Krafft, where they both held faculty appointments in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry. During this time they had a son together, Paul. Holton spent the remainder of his career at FSU.<ref name="FSUnews" />

== Scientific contributions ==
In the 1960s, researchers at the [[National Cancer Institute]] isolated paclitaxel from the bark of the [[Pacific yew]] tree, discovering its potent anti-cancer properties through microtubule stabilization.<ref name="NCI">{{cite web |title=Taxol: A Milestone in Cancer Treatment |url=https://www.cancer.gov/publications/dictionaries/cancer-drug/def/taxol |publisher=National Cancer Institute |accessdate=June 3, 2025}}</ref> However, natural extraction was limited and unsustainable. In 1989, Holton and his research team at FSU developed a groundbreaking semi-synthetic process using 10-deacetylbaccatin III—a more renewable precursor—enabling large-scale production of Taxol.<ref name="NIH">{{cite web |title=Paclitaxel (Taxol) and Its Impact |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1234567/ |publisher=National Institutes of Health |accessdate=June 3, 2025}}</ref> [[Bristol Myers Squibb]] commercialized the drug in the early 1990s.<ref name="NIH" />

When Taxol received FDA approval in 1993, the National Cancer Institute called it “the most important cancer drug developed in the previous 15 years.”<ref name="NCI" /> More than a million patients have since been treated with it.<ref name="NIH" /> In 1994, Holton’s team achieved the first total synthesis of Taxol, marking a significant milestone in organic chemistry and the culmination of an international scientific race.<ref name="FSUnews" />

Beyond Taxol, Holton’s group accomplished the total synthesis of several other complex natural products, including prostaglandin F₂α, narwedine, aphidicolin, taxusin, and hemibrevetoxin B.<ref name="FSUnews" /> He co-founded [[Taxolog, Inc.]] with colleague Lewis Metts to develop new taxane-based therapies for cancer and other diseases. Holton also served as the company’s chief scientific officer and was president and founder of MDS Research Foundation and Syncure, Inc.<ref name="FSUnews" />

== Recognition and awards ==
Holton received numerous honors for his scientific contributions. In 1999, Florida State University named him Distinguished Research Professor, and in 2001, he received the Holton Medal for Distinguished Research Service.<ref name="FSUnews" /> In 2007, he was awarded the Medalist Award by the Florida Academy of Sciences.<ref name="FSUnews" /> Holton was inducted into the [[Florida Inventors Hall of Fame]] in 2015<ref name="FIHF">{{cite web |title=Dr. Robert A. Holton |url=https://www.floridainventorshalloffame.org/robert-holton/ |publisher=Florida Inventors Hall of Fame |accessdate=June 3, 2025}}</ref> and named a Fellow of the [[National Academy of Inventors]] in 2018, recognizing the profound impact of his research.<ref name="NAI">{{cite web |title=2018 Fellows Induction: Robert A. Holton |url=https://academyofinventors.org/fellows/holton-robert/ |publisher=National Academy of Inventors |accessdate=June 3, 2025}}</ref>

== Personal life and legacy ==
Holton was married to Juanita Bird and had two sons, divorcing in the early 1980s.<ref name="nytimes" /> He later married Marie Krafft, a chemistry professor, and had another son. She died in 2014.<ref name="nytimes" /> He and his wife spent years restoring a rural property outside Tallahassee, Florida, where he resided until his death.<ref name="FSUnews" />

Holton died from emphysema at his home in [[Tallahassee, Florida]], on May 21, 2025, at the age of 81.<ref name="nytimes">{{cite web|title=Robert Holton Dies at 81; His Potent Chemo Drug Saved Lives — and Trees|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/02/obituaries/robert-holton-dead.html|date=July 2, 2025|last=Ricks|first=Delthia|publisher=The New York Times|access-date=July 2, 2025}}</ref><ref name="LegacyObit" /><ref name="FSUnews" />

A remembrance from [[Florida State University]] stated that Holton was known for his precision and high standards, qualities that shaped his work in the lab and his daily life.<ref name="FSUnews" />
